About this simulation

A quantum particle on a ring (\(R=1\); natural units \(\hbar=1\), \(2m=1\)) in periodic eigenstates labeled by the integer \(n\).

Physics

Energy \(E_n \propto n^2\), with lecture notation \(\psi_n(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi R}}e^{inx/R}\). The plot around the ring uses the angular coordinate \(\phi=x/R\). For \(n\neq 0\), \(\pm n\) are degenerate in energy.

\[E_n = \frac{n^2\hbar^2}{2mR^2}\]
\[\psi_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi R}} e^{inx/R}\]
\[P(x)=|\psi_n(x)|^2=\frac{1}{2\pi R}\]
Visuals

Energy levels: ladder of states vs energy; the chosen \(n\) is highlighted.
Wavefunction: real (blue) and imaginary (green) parts vs \(\phi\), or the same data wrapped on the ring; optional \(| \psi |^2\) band (yellow). Panels can be maximized.

Controls

Quantum Number: slider for \(n\); degeneracy note below it. Display Mode: ring vs \(\phi\) plot toggle; Show Re part / Show Im part; Show Probability Density \(|\psi|^2\); Animate Time Evolution. Visuals: Time Speed slider. Current State: ring radius, \(E_n\), wavelength, and the lecture equations. Top bar: Reset / Pause.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The ring

Here’s our playground. A particle moves freely on a circle of radius R — no walls, no forces, but the wave must join up with itself after one full turn. The energy ladder shows you which energies are allowed; beside it, the real (blue) and imaginary (green) parts of ψ are drawn around the ring. The integer n counts the whole wavelengths that fit into one circumference.

2 · The classical bead

Let’s start before quantum mechanics. A bead slides on a frictionless circular wire, with nothing to push it or slow it. Which energies do you think the bead can have?

3 · Whole numbers only

Now back to the quantum ring. Here the label n is restricted to integers. What do you think imposes that restriction?

4 · The lowest rung

Here’s something the box never allowed. A particle in a box can never have zero energy: there ψ would vanish everywhere. But the ring’s ladder has a rung at E = 0. What do you think that state looks like?

5 · Reversing the sign

Now let’s play with the sign. n may be negative as well as positive. Put side by side, how do you think the states n = +2 and n = −2 compare?

6 · Where is the particle?

One last look, and it’s a subtle one. The yellow band is |ψ|², the probability of finding the particle at each point. Take |n| from 2 up to 5. What’s your guess — how does that band change?

The Physics

The particle on a ring · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A particle on a ring feels no forces and meets no walls, yet its states form a set labelled by a number n. This sim shows each state twice: as a rung on an energy ladder, and as a wave drawn around the ring. It is the simplest model for ring-shaped molecules and tiny metal rings.

What you'll learn

  • What condition decides which waves are allowed on a ring, and what n counts.
  • How the wavelength, momentum and energy of a state depend on n.
  • How the states n and −n are related, and what the lowest state looks like.
  • What "stationary" means for a wave that moves around the ring, and what the probability density shows.
One state, shown the way the sim shows it: the wave around the ring, and its rung on the ladder.

What's on screen

  • Energy Levels (left panel): the rungs from n = 0 up to your |n|. Your rung is pink and drawn at the top, so the vertical scale changes with n.
  • Real part of ψ (blue), plotted against x from 0 to 2π (R = 1), or wrapped on the ring.
  • Imaginary part of ψ (green), drawn the same way.
  • Yellow band: the probability density |ψ|². On the ring view a dashed purple circle marks the ring itself.
  • Current State (sidebar): R, the energy En and the wavelength λ.
See itStart from the opening state, n = 1. Watch for: the pink rung at the top of the ladder, and the blue and green curves each making one wave across the plot.

03

Why the energies form a ladder

A bead on a frictionless wire can circle with any energy from zero upwards. A quantum particle on the ring is different because its wave must be single-valued: x and x + 2πR are the same point of the ring, so ψ has to return to its own value after one turn. With V = 0 the solutions are travelling waves:

Schrödinger's equation on the ring (V = 0), and its solutions. With R = 1 the arc length x and the angle φ are the same number.

Closing the wave onto itself keeps only whole numbers n, and the sign of n is allowed to be negative:

The condition is periodicity, not a wall: ψ does not have to vanish anywhere.
A wave that fits a whole number of times meets itself at the seam. At n = 2.5 it would return as −ψ. The sim offers only whole numbers.
Key idea. Nothing reflects the particle. The energies are restricted because the wave must close on itself.
See itFreeze the wave at n = 3 and read the two ends of the plot. Watch for: three whole waves between x = 0 and x = 2π, with each curve at the same height at both ends.
04

What n fixes: wavelength, momentum, energy

|n| whole wavelengths fit around the circumference 2πR. De Broglie's p = h/λ then gives the momentum, and on a ring momentum is angular momentum:

Wavelength, wave number, momentum and angular momentum from n.

With V = 0 all the energy is kinetic, so E = p²/2m:

The energy grows as n². The gap from rung |n| to the next one is (2|n| + 1) units.

Doubling |n| halves the wavelength, doubles the momentum and quadruples the energy. In the sim's units (ħ = 1, 2m = 1, R = 1) E is simply n².

n

This slider moves the sim too.

See itRun n = 2, then n = 4. Watch for: the Energy readout going from 4 to 16 while the wavelength halves.
05

The lowest rung is a flat wave

Periodicity allows n = 0. Then ψ₀ = 1/√(2πR) is a non-zero constant: it is normalised, it closes onto itself trivially, and it has E = 0, Lz = 0 and no wavelength (the sim prints "∞ (uniform)").

  • No zero-point energy. A particle in a box must have ψ = 0 at both walls, so a constant is not allowed and its lowest state costs π²ħ²/2mL². On the ring a constant is allowed, so the lowest energy is zero.
  • Normalisation. The density |ψ₀|² = 1/2πR, spread over the circumference 2πR, adds up to exactly 1.
  • One state. This is the only rung that is not shared. The badge under the slider reads "Non-Degenerate (n=0)".
See itSet n = 0. Watch for: the blue curve flat at the top tick (1/√2π), the green curve flat on the axis, and the ladder reduced to a single rung at E = 0.
06

n and −n share a rung

E = n²ħ²/2mR² does not see the sign of n, so E−n = En. The two states are still different: p = nħ/R and Lz = nħ have opposite signs, so the sign of n is the sense of circulation. Several states with one energy are called degenerate. Every rung except n = 0 holds two, and the sim's badge reads "Doubly Degenerate (±n)".

  • Frozen at t = 0 (Animate off): Re ψ = cos(nφ)/√2π is the same for ±n, and Im ψ = sin(nφ)/√2π changes sign.
  • Running: the whole pattern slides towards +φ (rightwards on the plot) for n > 0, and the other way for n < 0.
See itFreeze n = +3, switch to n = −3, then let it run. Watch for: the blue curve unchanged, the green curve flipped, the energy still 9, then the pattern sliding the opposite way.
07

A moving wave, a steady density

A state with energy En evolves by one rotating phase factor. The curves in the sim are the real and imaginary parts of Ψn, so Animate Time Evolution makes them slide round the ring. The probability density is Ψ times its complex conjugate, so the time-dependent phase cancels:

The density has no x in it and no t in it.
  • Stationary means |Ψ|² does not change in time. The curves move, but nothing you could measure does.
  • |Ψ|² = 1/2πR is a probability density: the chance of finding the particle in a short arc is this value times the arc's length. It is the same for every arc, and for every n.
  • Time Speed scales the screen clock only. The energy, the ladder and the band do not depend on it.
See itRun n = 5 with the yellow band on. Watch for: five waves sliding round the plot while the band stays at the same height.
08

Where it matters

Benzene as a ring of radius 0.139 nm: six π electrons fill n = 0 (two) and n = ±1 (four). The first empty rung is n = ±2.
  • Benzene. Treating its π electrons as free on a ring gives a first jump of about 5.9 eV, a photon near 210 nm. That lies in the ultraviolet region where benzene absorbs strongly, a fair estimate from a model with no chemistry in it.
  • Bohr's orbits. De Broglie's argument for Bohr's allowed orbits is this closing condition: 2πr = nλ gives L = nħ. Real atoms are three-dimensional, so the ring is only the starting idea.
  • Tiny metal rings. For a free electron on a ring of radius 50 nm, the first spacing is about 15 µeV (about 0.2 K), so experiments on such rings are done at millikelvin temperatures. Persistent currents set by a magnetic flux through the ring have been measured there.
Go deeper: mixtures of +n and −n, and a magnetic flux
  • Any mixture of ψn and ψ−n is also a state with energy En. The equal mixture is the standing wave cos(nφ)/√π, whose density has 2|n| peaks. The flat density of section 07 belongs to the circulating states the sim offers.
  • A flux Φ through the ring shifts the energies to E = (ħ²/2mR²)(n − Φ/Φ₀)², with Φ₀ = h/e for an electron. The ±n pair then splits, and the current no longer cancels.
09

Summary

In one line. A wave on a ring must close on itself, which allows only whole-number n, with E = n²ħ²/2mR², two states on every rung but the lowest, and a flat density.

Key points

  • ψ(x + 2πR) = ψ(x) restricts n to whole numbers, including 0 and negative values.
  • λ = 2πR/|n|, Lz = nħ and E ∝ n².
  • n = 0 is a constant wave with E = 0; ±n share a rung and circulate in opposite directions.
  • |ψ|² = 1/2πR for every circulating state.

Common mix-ups

  • "n = −3 sits lower than n = +3." E depends on n², so both are on the same rung. The sign sets the direction of circulation.
  • "At higher n the yellow band grows peaks." For the circulating states, |ψ|² = 1/2πR at every n. The curves wiggle faster, but their squares always add to a constant.
  • "The wave is moving, so the state can't be stationary." Stationary refers to |Ψ|², which does not change. The motion is a phase.

Things to try on your own

  • Step n from 0 up to 6 and write down E each time. Check that each gap is 2 larger than the one before.
  • Set n = 6 and count the blue curve's crests across the plot. Compare with the wavelength readout.
  • Turn Animate off and compare the Re and Im curves for n = 2 and n = −2.
